Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, told parents on November 29th, “We’ve got your back,” after pushing through some of the world’s strictest screentime limits. One year from now, under-16s will be banned from using social media, to protect them from harm. Teenagers groaned, parents discreetly high-fived, and policymakers took notes. Most social-media platforms forbid under-13s, following America’s 1998 COPPA (Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act) law on children’s online privacy. Britain’s Ofcom reports that 22% of users aged eight to 17 have an adult’s birth date. TikTok (minimum age: 13) is used by half of British eight- to 11-year-olds. Parents and politicians once turned a blind eye. But concern over social media’s mental-health impact is pushing governments to get tougher. Several European countries require parental permission for younger teens. Some American states have tried to limit teen usage. Australia, cheered on by its domestic press, is the first to enact a blanket ban.

Enforcement is the first challenge. Younger teenagers lack IDs like driving licences and credit cards, so companies often use machine learning to gauge age via selfies. Five years ago, such systems were off by about three years, says Tony Allen of the Age Check Certification Scheme, which works with the Australian government. Now, they can guess within about a year, better than most humans. Errors still happen, especially for people with darker skin, underrepresented in training data. Yoti, which checks ages for Meta, reports an average error of about a year for fair-skinned 13- to 17-year-olds, and 1.5 years for dark-skinned teens. Technical hurdles aside, how broad should the crackdown be? Social media spans everything from video to messaging. Australia says TikTok will fall under its ban, but YouTube will be exempt for its “significant” educational content. Video games are off the hook, though children now use platforms like Roblox to chat as well as play.

Another question is who should do the checks. Australia puts the onus on social-media platforms: “You create the risk, you’ve got to deal with it,” says Mr Allen. Meta and others argue operating systems or app stores should handle age verification. That would let phones vouch for users’ ages anonymously, instead of people handing over IDs to every network. But governments are wary of forcing Apple or Google to build global ID registries. Age limits will affect some platforms more than others. Checks will cost startups more (Yoti quotes 3-31 cents per check). Whereas only 5% of Facebook’s American users are under 18, 19% of Snapchat’s are. Young users are not especially valuable to advertisers: Brian Wieser of Madison and Wall estimates under-16 ads form a “low single-digit percentage” of spending. Meta has not shown ads to under-18s in the EU for more than a year, amid legal disputes, with little impact.

No one knows how much banning teens will reduce their interest as adults. But TikTok, already threatened with a US ban, could be disadvantaged if teenagers cannot use it while rivals like YouTube remain accessible. The big winners of this crackdown may be gaming, so long as the ban does not expand further. Many now watch to see its global impact.
passages.V2:
[In 1968, Paul and Anne Ehrlich’s The Population Bomb predicted mass starvation due to overpopulation, yet by 1990, global famine had largely been averted, and living standards had improved.] … Yet one might also say, in hindsight, that the Ehrlichs were only wrong about which species would starve. In the second half of the 20th century, global human famine was averted by the Green Revolution’s formula of high-yield, semi-dwarf cereal varieties, synthetic fertilizers, chemical pesticides, monocrop agriculture, and intensified irrigation. These advances helped save perhaps two billion lives, yet the planet bears the costs of this so-called miracle. The Ehrlichs failed to predict that while humans survived, countless species and ecosystems would be pushed to the brink of collapse.

The Green Revolution’s reliance on pesticides and habitat destruction has triggered a mass die-off of insects at an alarming rate of 2.5 percent per year. This decline threatens birds, fish, amphibians, and mammals that rely on them. Meanwhile, carbon emissions have raised global temperatures by 0.15 to 0.20 degrees Celsius every decade since 1975. These emissions have also rendered the oceans 26 percent more acidic than they were in the Holocene, endangering marine life. Coral reefs, which support one in four marine species, are collapsing. Similarly, a fifth of the Amazon rainforest has been clear-cut, largely for cattle ranching. Today, eco-leftists acknowledge that population growth itself does not drive climate change. Instead, the primary driver is the Global North’s insatiable consumption, shaped by capitalism’s vision of the good life: suburban mansions, luxury vacations, airmailed delicacies, and oversized SUVs. Unlike the Ehrlichs, contemporary “degrowth” advocates … argue for reducing economic growth in wealthy nations while redistributing resources to the Global South.

Yet, the broader debate remains unresolved: Is our relationship with the planet primarily a story of scarcity, where insatiable human wants clash with finite resources? Or is it one of human ingenuity, where new technologies continuously unlock fresh abundance? This debate is overshadowed by its most infamous participants. Anyone who questions unchecked growth risks being labeled an “Ehrlichian” or a “neo-Malthusian”—a reference to the 19th-century demographer Thomas Malthus, who opposed aid to the poor, believing it would lead to overpopulation. To question economic expansion, then, is to risk association with historically discredited figures.

This is why Fredrik Albritton Jonsson and Carl Wennerlind’s new intellectual history, Scarcity: A History from the Origins of Capitalism to the Climate Crisis, is timely. The authors argue that discussions about scarcity have a much richer and more ethically nuanced history than contemporary economic debates suggest. Beyond pessimistic doomsayers like Ehrlich and Malthus, thinkers across centuries have grappled with how society should balance needs, desires, and available resources. One particularly striking example is John Stuart Mill. Unlike many classical economists, Mill envisioned a future where nations would eventually cease reinvesting profits in endless growth and instead embrace a “stationary state”—an economy of sufficiency rather than relentless expansion. He questioned the capitalist treadmill of competition, where people are condemned to a life of “trampling, crushing, elbowing, and treading on each other’s heels.” More than a century ago, Mill foresaw the dangers of unchecked industrial expansion—not just for humanity, but for the natural world.
passages.V3:
All human languages follow the same pattern: The most common word is used twice as often as the second most common word, three times as often as the third… and so on. This statistical rule is called Zipf’s law, and now an interdisciplinary team of scientists has shown that humpback whale songs follow the same pattern. … Researchers suggest this might have developed because it makes culturally transmitted communication—such as language and whale song—easier to learn. “It strengthens the view that we should be thinking about human language not as a completely different phenomenon from other communication systems but instead think about what it shares with them,” says one psychologist involved in the research. How to search for the pattern in whale song wasn’t immediately clear. … First, the team had to identify the units within the song that would be equivalent to words. They were inspired by how babies learn language.

“Speech is continuous… infants have to discover word boundaries,” one researcher explains. “They use low-level statistical information: sounds are more likely to occur together if they are part of the same word. Infants use dips in the probability that one sound follows another to discover word boundaries.” For example, children could identify the distinct words in the phrase “after dinner” by noting that certain syllables do not usually go together. … “If whale song has a similar statistical structure,” the researcher adds, “these cues should be useful for segmenting it as well.” Using this method, the team analyzed eight years of humpback whale song data, plotting the frequency of sounds and word-like sequences—including syllables described as “grunt,” “descending high squeak” and “ascending moan.” … They discovered that humpback whale songs also follow Zipf’s law. “I’ll never forget the moment that graph appeared, looking just like the one we know so well from human language,” says another researcher. “We realized we’d uncovered a deep commonality between two species separated by tens of millions of years of evolution.”

Why would two species both develop communication that follows Zipf’s law? … The researchers suggest it might be because it makes the form of communication—whether it’s language or song—easier to pass on to future generations. Their findings indicate that whale songs may have culturally evolved to be easier for novices to learn, echoing how human languages seem to evolve toward greater learnability. … With future research, scientists hope to find these properties in other culturally transmitted systems of sequential signaling, such as those of bats, songbirds, or elephants. In another study, researchers found two additional shared features between human language and whale communication: Menzerath’s law… which holds that longer sequences tend to have shorter words. Previously, scientists discovered similar patterns in jackass penguins… which were shown to follow these laws, too. However, whale song is not equivalent to human language, largely because it lacks expressive meaning. Humpback whale song could be comparable to human music, which also lacks semantic meaning while still adhering to Zipf’s law. But it challenges long-held assumptions about human language and reveals deep commonalities.
passages.V4:
What is fantasy for? You do not suddenly start needing philosophy when you turn eighteen: you have always needed it. Fantasy is philosophy’s more gorgeously painted cousin. You can’t just tell a child a blunt fact about the human heart and expect them to believe you. That’s not how it works. You can’t scribble on a Post-it note for a 12-year-old: your strangeness is worth keeping, or your love will matter. You need to show it. And fantasy, with its limitless scope, gives us a way of offering longhand proof for otherwise inarticulable ideas: endurance, hatred, regret, power, passion, death. As Tolkien said, ‘human stories are practically always about one thing, aren’t they? Death. The inevitability of death.’

For more than three thousand years we have been inventing mythical creatures, though why is less clear. One theory is that we built creatures to match inexplicable remains we found. The Indigenous American mythological beast, the Thunder Bird, may have stemmed from T-Rex skeletons. Adrienne Mayor has pointed to many instances where fossil discoveries map onto local mythmaking: ‘Someone who discovered a tyrannosaurid forelimb... might well have identified the fossil as part of some mysterious bird.’ Shark teeth left over from Neanderthal meals have been read as dragon teeth.

I’ve spent years reading about mythical beasts for my book Impossible Creatures, and what’s striking is how blurry the line has been between real and imagined. In Pliny the Elder’s Natural History - often called the first encyclopedia - there is a description of the jaculus dragon. The theologian Felix Fabri reported glimpsing a unicorn in the Sinai desert, its horn ‘wondrous brilliant.’ And if you lived back then, you might have believed griffins were real; King Charles I’s chaplain, Alexander Ross, said: ‘If any man say that now such animals are not to be seen; I answer... they may be removed to places inaccessible to men.’ Not everyone loves a dragon. There are many attacks you can level at fantasy: escapist, ridiculous, indulgent, coy, repetitive. One of the Inklings - nobody agrees which - is supposed to have groaned at Tolkien’s reading: ‘By god, not another bloody elf!’ With its limitless possibilities, fantasy has lured some of the worst writing. There are books that give you nothing except relentless battles, didactic hectoring or crass sentimentalism - but then there are many very bad songs, and it does not turn us off the concept of music. There are many bad dinners, but it does not turn us off feasting.

At its best, you can turn to fantasy, especially for children, for the essence of things. Ursula Le Guin takes her guiding line from Tolkien, who never sought to deny that fantasy is escapist: that is its power and glory. ‘If a soldier is imprisoned by the enemy, don’t we consider it his duty to escape? The moneylenders, the know-nothings, the authoritarians have us all in prison; if we value freedom of mind and soul, if we’re partisans of liberty, it’s our plain duty to escape, and to take as many people with us as we can.’

Buoyancy is the ability to navigate moral conflict without being overwhelmed, maintaining clarity and stability. It helps clinicians face ethical challenges without being debilitated and fosters growth through adversity. Cultivating self-regulation and awareness enhances buoyancy by enabling recognition of heightened emotional, mental, and physical states, allowing a shift toward insight and stability. Over time, this process strengthens neural pathways, improving resilience in ethical dilemmas. When clinicians’ nervous systems are dysregulated, they struggle to perceive ethical challenges clearly and act with integrity. Without mindfulness practices to stabilize their system, they become vulnerable to the effects of sustained stress, making ethical decision-making more difficult. Developing buoyancy ensures clinicians can maintain balance and respond effectively to moral adversity.

Buoyancy enables clinicians to navigate ethical dilemmas with clarity and stability, improving resilience through self-regulation and mindfulness.
Maintaining buoyancy in ethical dilemmas requires clinicians to develop self-regulation and mindfulness, preventing stress from impairing moral clarity.
Buoyancy, strengthened by self-regulation and neural adaptation, allows clinicians to maintain ethical integrity and resilience in the face of moral adversity.

Social change is rarely epochal, and epochs are bigger than presidential administrations. Decades of political policy create social structures that engender tendencies that are hard to break, even when we want to. Future events are deeply rooted in past conditions…In times of moral panic and ontological fear, it is only human to want to take control of time, to declare the end or beginning of something. Which is to say that, when our present feels disjointed, we try to break history at its joints.
opts: While social change unfolds gradually over time, fear and moral panic push people to declare the beginning or end of an era, even when history resists such divisions.
Epochal change is rare, as deeply embedded social structures evolve over decades, though in uncertain times, people attempt to break history into distinct periods.
Despite history’s continuous nature, people in times of crisis seek control by creating artificial historical divides, believing they can separate the past from the present.
Social change is a gradual process shaped by political and historical forces, yet in moments of fear and crisis people try to impose artificial breaks in history.

Negative theology is an outgrowth of mysticism. Mystical experiences, as defined by William James in The Varieties of Religious Experience, possess two seemingly contradictory properties. They are on the one hand “noetic,” that is, you feel you are gaining profound insight into and knowledge of reality. They are on the other hand “ineffable,” meaning you cannot convey your revelation in words. Mystical aphorisms often emphasize ineffability. “He who knows, does not speak,” the ancient Chinese sage Lao Tzu says, violating his own dictum. “He who speaks, does not know.” Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a medieval monk, describes mystical knowledge as being “at one with Him Who is indescribable.”
opts: Mysticism, central to negative theology, involves experiences that are both profoundly revelatory and ineffable, as seen in the teachings of Lao Tzu and Pseudo-Dionysius.
Negative theology, rooted in mystical traditions, grapples with the paradox of mystical experiences being both illuminating and beyond verbal expression.
Negative theology emerges from mysticism, which presents a paradox: mystical experiences feel deeply insightful yet cannot be expressed in words.
The mystical foundation of negative theology lies in the tension between insight and ineffability, a contradiction explored in religious teachings.

Paragraph: Poland has been a key supporter of Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion began. ___(1)___ It serves as the main logistics hub for military and humanitarian aid entering Ukraine. Poland has also been a strong advocate that Russia must not be allowed to win, arguing that all of Europe’s security is at stake. There is growing concern that the U.S. appears to be conceding to Moscow’s key demands even before talks begin. ___(2)___ Poland sees Russia as the clear aggressor and a serious threat. This is why Poland invests heavily in its military, now spending nearly 5% of GDP. ___(3)___ Ahead of the Paris talks, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote on X: "If we, Europeans, fail to spend big on defence now, we will be forced to spend 10 times more if we don't prevent a wider war." ___(4)___ On the issue of sending Polish troops to Ukraine to help enforce a ceasefire, government officials remain cautious. For now, they have ruled it out.

23.q:
Five jumbled-up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

Its success would depend significantly on ensuring that people with disabilities participate in every phase of the design process.

To make the most of universal inclusion, financial institutions should embrace a new innovation framework built on accessibility.

This would represent a significant shift from today’s compliance-based approach, in which adjustments are often made after the fact to meet minimum accessibility standards.

Measuring our progress on overall financial inclusion is important, but so is collecting detailed data that differentiate among groups or segments.

In a universally inclusive design approach, accessibility considerations should shape solutions from the start.

24.q:
Five jumbled-up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

The second occurred in 1989, with the fall of the Berlin Wall marking the West’s victory in the Cold War.

It is a multipolar world, with China, Russia, India, Turkey, Brazil, South Africa, and the Gulf states challenging the old order, alongside other emerging powers demanding a greater voice in shaping the rules of the international system.

“The old world is dying, and the new world struggles to be born: now is the time of monsters.”

That order has been shaped by two pivotal historical moments, the first came after 1945, when the current international system was established through the creation of the United Nations and the Bretton Woods institutions.

This famous quote, often attributed to Antonio Gramsci, feels particularly pertinent today, as the international order that has defined the past century undergoes a profound shift.
